newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian government sued by "stolen" Aborigines.
newsitem.headline: Australian government sued by "stolen" Aborigines.

text.p: A group of 550 "Stolen Generation" Aborigines who were forcibly removed as children from their parents under an official assimilation policy began legal action on Wednesday against the Australian government.
Lawyers representing the 550 Aborigines and 11 aboriginal mothers lodged writs in the Darwin High Court in the Northern Territory.

The writs seek unspecified damages, arguing the government "recklessly and negligently breached the duty of care owed to the children in its custody, causing injury, loss and damage to the plaintiffs".
"We have been given no option but to seek justice through our court system," said David Guy from the Stolen Generation Litigation Unit.
"We now urge all our fellow Australians to open their ears and their hearts as we tell our stories in the months ahead," Guy said in a statement from Darwin.

Tens of thousands of Aborigines were forcibly separated from their families and placed in state and church care centres under the government policy which ended in the mid-1960s. Many were physically and sexually abused.

Aborigines who were taken away call themselves the "Stolen Generation" and describe the forced separation policy as "genocide" because it aimed to assimilate Aborigines into Australia's then predominantly Anglo-Saxon society.
Some of Australia's most prominent Aborigines were separated from their parents, including Lois O'Donoghue, head of the nation's top aboriginal body.
The separation policy, under which children were either never told or told late in life that they were Aborigines, has resulted in generations of dysfunctional aboriginal families.
An inquiry into 99 aboriginal deaths in police custody in the 1980s found 43 of the Aborigines who died had been separated from their families as children.
An official government-sponsored inquiry into the "Stolen Generation" will issue a report next year and is expected to recommend financial compensation.

Australian Prime Minister John Howard has said he sees no need for compensation to be paid, arguing that the money could be better spent improving indigenous health and education. There are about 300,000 Aborigines in Australia out of a total population of 18 million.
A group of six mixed-race Northern Territory Aborigines is already suing the government. Guy said he hoped more lawsuits would follow across Australia.
"We are committed to seeing this litigation through to a successful conclusion and hope it will inspire Stolen Generations in other states to commence similar legal action," he said.
